Intuitively, when I picture a grid turned into graph representation, clearly, external (corners and sides) and internal positions reflect on the valence of the nodes. 

Now, in the case of a maze, certain positions are blocked off thus the adjacency is meaningless from a mobility perspective. 

The mobility graph now is more interesting. Namely, a non-trial grid graph with holes in it.

I might be tempted to use this representation as a way to visualize various stats of stigmergy or other protocol phenomena.

(Possibly relevant to, [Umwelt](https://thoughtfolio.xyz/Protocol+Theory/Stigmergy+Workshop/Ontology+of+a+Semantic+Engine+for+World+Simulations+and+Protocol+Studies))
content_html:
I just remember something I wanted to pin for a later exploration.

Explore the connection between "Mazes" and their graph representations built out of adjacency relations.

The work we have done on stigsim lead me to understand how much can be done on top of discrete topologies, like grids when you instantiate something like a maze on top of it.

Intuitively, when I picture a grid turned into graph representation, clearly, external (corners and sides) and internal positions reflect on the valence of the nodes.

Now, in the case of a maze, certain positions are blocked off thus the adjacency is meaningless from a mobility perspective.

The mobility graph now is more interesting. Namely, a non-trial grid graph with holes in it.

I might be tempted to use this representation as a way to visualize various stats of stigmergy or other protocol phenomena.

(Possibly relevant to, Umwelt)
